items.title: Security Breach Notification Act
items.applies_to_vendor: An individual or entity that maintains computerized data containing personal information that it does not own must notify the owner or licensee of the information of a breach following discovery, per the Act's notice framework (24 O.S. §163); an entity that maintains its own compliant notification/security policy, or is regulated under GLBA, HIPAA, the Oklahoma Hospital Cybersecurity Protection Act of 2023, or a federal functional regulator, is deemed compliant (24 O.S. §164).
key_obligations: Entities that own or license computerized personal information must disclose a breach to affected Oklahoma residents (24 O.S. §163).
Entities that maintain (but do not own) the data must notify the data owner/licensee of the breach (24 O.S. §163).

An entity with its own notification procedures consistent with the Act's timing requirements, or regulated under GLBA/HIPAA/the Oklahoma Hospital Cybersecurity Protection Act of 2023/a federal functional regulator, is deemed compliant (24 O.S. §164).

Did not independently fetch §163 (core duty/deadline text) or §165 (penalties/AG threshold) from an official page this session, so exact deadline wording, AG-notice threshold, and penalty cap are left blank here rather than guessed, per the no-fabrication rule; secondary sources report a deadline of 'most expedient time possible' and a penalty cap near $150,000 per breach, unconfirmed.

items.title: Student Data Accessibility, Transparency and Accountability Act of 2013
items.applies_to_vendor: Contracts that govern databases, assessments, or instructional supports containing student or de-identified data and that are outsourced to private vendors must include express provisions safeguarding privacy and security and penalties for vendor noncompliance.
key_obligations: The State Board of Education must adopt rules/policies implementing student-data privacy and security under the Act.
Vendor contracts involving student or de-identified data must include express privacy/security safeguard provisions and penalties for noncompliance.
The State Department of Education must maintain ongoing FERPA and related privacy-law compliance, including compliance audits.
items.penalties: Vendor contracts must include penalties for noncompliance; the statute itself does not specify a fixed penalty amount per available summaries.

items.title: Oklahoma Data Privacy Act (SB 546)
items.citation: SB 546 (2026), expected codification 75A Okla. Stat. §§ 300-315 per secondary trackers
items.applies_to_vendor: Processors (vendors acting on behalf of a controller) are subject to the comprehensive-privacy-law processor model of controller instructions and a written processing contract; LOVELEEDAY acting as a data processor for an Oklahoma-facing client would need a compliant data processing agreement in place before the January 1, 2027 effective date.
key_obligations: Applies to businesses that process personal data of 100,000+ Oklahoma consumers, or 25,000+ consumers while deriving a majority of revenue from selling personal data.
Businesses must provide transparent privacy notices, maintain reasonable data security practices, and obtain consent before processing sensitive personal information.
Grants consumers rights to access, correct, delete, and obtain copies of personal data, and to opt out of sale of data and targeted advertising.
Exempts state agencies, nonprofits, higher-education institutions, and data already regulated under federal law such as HIPAA.
Enforced exclusively by the Oklahoma Attorney General.

items.title: Oregon Consumer Identity Theft Protection Act - Notice of Breach of Security
items.applies_to_vendor: A 'vendor' (a person that maintains, stores, manages, processes, or otherwise possesses personal information on behalf of a covered entity) must notify the contracting covered entity of a breach as soon as practicable and not later than 10 days after discovery; the covered entity is then responsible for notifying affected consumers.
key_obligations: Covered entities must notify affected consumers in the most expeditious manner possible, without unreasonable delay, and not later than 45 days after discovery or receipt of a vendor's breach notice.
Vendors must notify the contracting covered entity as soon as practicable, not later than 10 days after discovering the breach.

Covered entities must notify the Attorney General if more than 250 consumers are affected; vendors must notify the AG if more than 250 consumers (or an undeterminable number) were affected and the covered entity has not already reported.
Notice must include a description of the breach, approximate date, categories of information involved, contact information, and advice to contact nationwide consumer reporting agencies and the FTC.
items.notice_deadline: "as soon as is practicable but not later than 45 days" after discovery (covered entity); vendor to covered entity "as soon as is practicable but not later than 10 days" after discovery
items.regulator_notice: Attorney General must be notified when more than 250 consumers are affected.
items.penalties: Violations are unlawful trade practices under ORS 646.607, enforceable by the Attorney General.
items.uncertainty: The state's own oregonlegislature.gov index page (fetched this session) confirms the section exists and its official title; its full operative text sits in a separate chapter PDF not opened directly this session. The specific deadline wording, AG threshold, and notice-content requirements above were read from the oregon.public.law mirror (a widely used, non-governmental restatement of the ORS) rather than the state's raw text.

items.title: Oregon Student Information Protection Act
items.applies_to_vendor: An 'operator' of a website/service/application designed and marketed for K-12 school purposes may not engage in targeted advertising, build student profiles using persistent identifiers, or sell covered student information; disclosure to a contracted service provider is permitted only under a contract prohibiting further disclosure and requiring reasonable security procedures.
key_obligations: Operators may not use covered information for targeted advertising on their own or other sites/services.
Operators may not sell student personal information (subject to a narrow merger/acquisition exception).
Operators may not build a profile of a student using persistent identifiers except for K-12 purposes.
Operators must implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the sensitivity of the data.
Operators must delete covered student information within a reasonable time upon a school's request.
Disclosure to a service provider is permitted only under a contract prohibiting further disclosure and requiring reasonable security.
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Covers educational records, contact details, discipline records, test scores, health data, biometric information, and geolocation data tied to a K-12 student.
items.penalties: Violations are treated as unlawful business practices under Oregon law.

Full operative text (prohibitions, security/deletion duties) was read from the oregon.public.law mirror rather than the state's own PDF text this session; treat exact wording as a paraphrase pending direct confirmation against the state's raw statute PDF. items.title: Oregon Consumer Privacy Act
items.applies_to_vendor: A processor (entity that processes personal data on behalf of a controller, e.g., LOVELEEDAY acting as a vendor to its clients) must adhere to the controller's instructions and operate under a contract with the controller (ORS 646A.581) governing processing instructions, confidentiality, deletion/return of data, and assistance with the controller's compliance obligations (security, breach notice, data protection assessments).
key_obligations: 646A.578: Controllers must limit data collection, provide a privacy notice, and honor consumer rights (access, correction, deletion, portability, opt-out of targeted advertising/sale/profiling).

646A.581: Processor duties are governed by a binding contract with the controller covering processing instructions, confidentiality, subcontractor flow-down, deletion/return of data, and audit/assistance obligations; a processor that begins determining the purposes of processing becomes a controller.
646A.586: Controllers must conduct data protection assessments for processing that presents heightened risk of harm.
646A.589: The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority, including investigative demand power and civil penalties.
items.penalties: Attorney General enforcement with civil penalties under ORS 646A.589; exact penalty amount not confirmed this session.
items.uncertainty: oregonlegislature.gov (official, fetched this session) confirms the section list and titles for 646A.570-589. Effective date and detailed obligations above are corroborated by the Oregon DOJ consumer-protection page and Oregon Real Estate Agency newsroom (both official .gov, identified but not independently opened this session) plus secondary trackers; exact penalty figures were not confirmed via direct fetch.

items.title: Breach of Personal Information Notification Act
items.applies_to_vendor: A vendor/third party that maintains, stores, or manages computerized data on behalf of another entity must notify that entity of a breach; the entity that owns/licenses the data is responsible for notifying affected Pennsylvania residents without unreasonable delay following determination of the breach.
key_obligations: Any entity that maintains, stores, or manages computerized data including personal information must notify affected PA residents of a breach without unreasonable delay following determination.

State agencies, agency contractors, counties, public schools, and municipalities must notify within seven business days of determination; counties/school districts must also notify the district attorney within 3 business days.
The Attorney General must be notified when a breach affects more than 500 Pennsylvania residents.
A violation is an unfair or deceptive act under the Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law, enforced exclusively by the Attorney General.
items.notice_deadline: "without unreasonable delay" following determination of the breach (state agencies/political subdivisions: "within seven business days following determination")
items.regulator_notice: Attorney General notice required when a breach affects more than 500 Pennsylvania residents.
items.personal_info_definition_notes: First name/initial + last name combined with unencrypted/unredacted SSN, driver's license/ID number, financial account/card number with security code, medical information, health insurance information, or online account credentials.
items.penalties: Enforced as an unfair/deceptive practice under the Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law; Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority.
items.uncertainty: Fetched the official Pennsylvania General Assembly text (legis.state.pa.us) this session; its own citations show amendment through 2024 (Act 33) and 2022 (Act 151). Exact current section numbering (2301-2308 range, including 5.1-5.4 amendments) is a reconstruction from the fetched content and should be spot-checked against the fully consolidated current text.

items.title: Identity Theft Protection Act of 2015 - Notification of Breach
items.applies_to_vendor: Any municipal agency, state agency, or person (including a vendor/processor) that stores, owns, collects, processes, maintains, acquires, uses, or licenses personal information must notify Rhode Island residents of a breach that poses a significant risk of identity theft.
key_obligations: Businesses/persons must notify affected RI residents no later than 45 calendar days after confirmation of the breach; government agencies must notify within 30 calendar days.
When more than 500 RI residents are affected, the entity must also notify the Attorney General and major nationwide credit reporting agencies as to the timing, content, and distribution of notices.

Notification may be delayed at the request of a law enforcement agency that determines it would impede a criminal investigation; the agency must notify of the delay request without unreasonable delay.
Failure to notify makes the entity liable for a violation under R.I. Gen. Laws §11-49.3-5.
items.notice_deadline: "no later than forty-five (45) calendar days after confirmation of the breach" (persons/businesses); "no later than thirty (30) calendar days" (state/municipal agencies)
items.regulator_notice: Attorney General and nationwide credit reporting agencies must be notified when more than 500 Rhode Island residents are affected.
items.penalties: Violation liability under R.I. Gen. Laws §11-49.3-5 (not independently confirmed this session).
items.effective_or_amended: 2015 (recodified as the Identity Theft Protection Act of 2015)
items.uncertainty: Fetched directly from the official Rhode Island General Assembly statute server this session; §11-49.3-5 (penalties) was referenced but not independently opened.

items.title: Student Data - Cloud Computing
items.applies_to_vendor: A cloud computing service provider contracting with a school/school district may process K-12 student data solely to provide the contracted service and may not process it for any commercial purpose, including advertising; the provider must certify in writing that it will comply with the section.
key_obligations: Cloud computing providers must process K-12 student data solely for the purpose of providing the contracted cloud computing service.
Providers are barred from processing student data for any commercial purpose, including advertising.
Providers must certify in writing that they will comply with the section.
items.uncertainty: Fetched directly from the official Rhode Island General Assembly statute server this session. This single-section chapter does not itself specify security standards, data-deletion timelines, or penalties for violation - none invented here.

items.title: Rhode Island Data Transparency and Privacy Protection Act
items.applies_to_vendor: A processor (vendor acting on behalf of a controller) has responsibilities under §6-48.1-7 (Controller and processor responsibilities). Personal data regulated by FERPA is exempt from the Act, so K-12 vendor relationships are governed instead by Rhode Island's student-data statutes rather than this Act.
key_obligations: §6-48.1-3: Governs information-sharing practices.
§6-48.1-4: Governs processing of information.
§§6-48.1-5/6: Establish and govern the exercise of consumer rights.
§6-48.1-7: Sets controller and processor responsibilities.
§6-48.1-8: Violations, enforced by the Attorney General.
Personal data regulated by FERPA (20 U.S.C. §1232g) is exempt from the Act.
items.penalties: Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority; secondary sources report violations are treated as deceptive trade practices with civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation, not independently confirmed via direct fetch of §6-48.1-8 this session.

items.title: Breach of Security of Business Data
items.applies_to_vendor: A person conducting business in South Carolina and owning or licensing computerized personal identifying information must disclose a breach to affected residents when illegal use has occurred or is reasonably likely, or when there is a material risk of harm.
key_obligations: A person conducting business in SC that owns or licenses computerized personal identifying information must disclose a breach to affected residents when illegal use has occurred or is reasonably likely, or when there is a material risk of harm.
Notice must be made in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, consistent with legitimate law-enforcement needs.
When more than 1,000 persons are notified at one time, the business must also notify the SC Department of Consumer Affairs' Consumer Protection Division and nationwide consumer reporting agencies.
Banks/financial institutions subject to and compliant with GLBA privacy/security provisions are exempt.
items.notice_deadline: "in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, consistent with the legitimate needs of law enforcement"
items.regulator_notice: SC Department of Consumer Affairs, Consumer Protection Division, must be notified when more than 1,000 persons are notified at one time.
items.personal_info_definition_notes: First name/initial + last name combined with SSN, driver's license/state ID number, financial account/card number with security code, or other government ID numbers that uniquely identify an individual, when unencrypted/unredacted.
items.penalties: Administrative fine of $1,000 per affected resident for knowing/willful violations; private right of action for actual damages (negligent violations) and broader recovery for knowing/willful violations; injunctive relief and attorney's fees/costs available.
items.effective_or_amended: Enacted 2008 (Act No. 190, effective July 1, 2009); amended 2013 (Act No. 15, effective April 23, 2013)

items.title: South Dakota data breach notification law
items.applies_to_vendor: An information holder conducting business in South Dakota that owns or licenses computerized personal or protected information of SD residents must disclose a breach; an information holder regulated by a federal functional regulator is deemed compliant if it follows its federal breach procedures and notifies SD residents accordingly.
key_obligations: Disclosure must be made no later than 60 days from discovery or notification of the breach, unless a longer period is needed for legitimate law-enforcement purposes.
The Attorney General must be notified by mail or email of any breach affecting more than 250 South Dakota residents.

Notification is not required if, after investigation and AG notification, the information holder reasonably determines the breach is not likely to result in harm; that determination must be documented and retained for at least 3 years.
Penalties reach up to $10,000 per day per violation for noncompliance.
items.notice_deadline: "no later than sixty days from the discovery or notification of the breach of system security", unless a longer period is required for legitimate law-enforcement needs
items.regulator_notice: Attorney General must be notified of any breach exceeding 250 South Dakota residents.
items.penalties: Up to $10,000 per day per violation.

items.title: Identity Theft Deterrence Act - Release of Personal Consumer Information
items.applies_to_vendor: An 'information holder' who maintains (but does not own) computerized personal information must notify the data's owner/licensee of a breach following discovery, consistent with the Act's disclosure timing requirements.
key_obligations: Information holders must disclose a breach of the security of the system to affected Tennessee residents whose unencrypted personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person.
Disclosure must be made no later than 45 days from discovery or notification of the breach, unless a longer period is required due to legitimate law-enforcement needs.
If notification is delayed for law enforcement, it must be made no later than 45 days after law enforcement determines notification will not compromise the investigation.

If more than 1,000 persons must be notified at one time, the information holder must also notify, without unreasonable delay, all nationwide consumer reporting agencies/credit bureaus of the timing, distribution, and content of the notices.
items.notice_deadline: "no later than forty-five (45) days from the discovery or notification of the breach of system security", unless a longer period is required due to the legitimate needs of law enforcement
items.personal_info_definition_notes: A breach of the security of the system means unauthorized acquisition of unencrypted computerized data that materially compromises the security, confidentiality, or integrity of personal information maintained by the information holder.
items.effective_or_amended: Amended 2016 and 2017 (added the firm 45-day deadline and encryption-related provisions)
items.uncertainty: Tennessee's official codified statutes are published exclusively through LexisNexis under contract with the Tennessee Code Commission (no free .gov full-text HTML exists). Used the Tennessee Attorney General's own consumer-law resource page (tn.gov/attorneygeneral, official, fetched this session) as the source, which cites §47-18-2107 and the 45-day timeline directly. Regulator-notice and penalty provisions were not addressed on that page and are left null rather than guessed.

items.title: Tennessee Information Protection Act (TIPA)
items.applies_to_vendor: Processors must follow controller instructions, assist with consumer-rights requests, and provide information enabling the controller's data-protection assessments, under a written contract between controller and processor; LOVELEEDAY acting as processor for a covered client would need such a contract in place.
key_obligations: Applies to businesses that do business in TN or target TN residents, have $25M+ annual revenue, and either (a) control/process 25,000+ TN consumers' data and derive 50%+ of gross revenue from selling personal data, or (b) control/process 175,000+ TN consumers' data annually.

Controllers must provide accessible privacy notices, limit data collection to what is reasonably necessary, implement reasonable security practices, avoid unlawful discriminatory processing, and obtain consent before processing sensitive data.
Processors must follow controller instructions, assist with consumer-rights requests and data-protection assessments, and operate under a written processor contract.

The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority; entities receive written notice and a 60-day cure period before an action; an affirmative defense exists for businesses maintaining a privacy program that reasonably conforms to the NIST Privacy Framework.
Exempts political subdivisions, financial institutions, HIPAA-covered entities, nonprofits, and higher-education institutions.
items.penalties: Attorney General enforcement following a 60-day cure period; specific civil penalty amount not confirmed this session.
items.uncertainty: Sourced from the Tennessee Attorney General's own TIPA guidance press release (tn.gov/attorneygeneral, official, fetched in full this session), which confirms citation, effective date, thresholds, exemptions, controller/processor duties, and the cure-period/NIST affirmative defense. Exact civil-penalty dollar amount was not stated on that page and is left null rather than guessed.
